title: Hillel on one foot
hookLine: asked to teach the whole Torah on one foot, Hillel says: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, the rest is commentary, go and learn (Talmud, Shabbat 31a)

cards: Somebody asks you to explain your whole job, your whole faith, your whole life's philosophy, in one sentence. Go. Right now.

It's a slightly rude question, and a slightly brilliant one. Two thousand years ago, in Jerusalem, a man walked up to two of the greatest rabbis of his day with a version of it. The Talmud tells the story.
He said: teach me the entire Torah, all of it, while I stand on one foot. The first rabbi, Shammai, chased him away. The second was Hillel.

teach.b: It's in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page thirty-one. A man who isn't Jewish asks Shammai to teach him the whole Torah on one foot.
Shammai, well known for it, strict, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick he's holding. So he tries Hillel. Hillel doesn't send him away.
He answers in Aramaic, short enough to say standing on one foot.

teach.h: WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.
teach.b: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah.
The rest is commentary. Now go and learn. Three things happen in that answer.

The Talmud doesn't name a verse here, but many readers hear behind it the commandment in Leviticus, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society wording, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," put in its most practical form: don't do to others what you hate.
You met a version of this on day fifteen of this path, the golden rule, and it lives in many traditions. Second, the rest is commentary: not unimportant, but built around that center.
Third, the part people forget: now go and learn.

teach.h: THE ONE LINE ISN'T THE END.
teach.b: Hillel doesn't say the one line is enough. He gives the summary, then sends the man to study.
The whole teaching fits on one foot. Living it takes two feet and the rest of your life. Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says, often disagreed, and their schools argued for generations.
Jewish tradition kept both sides of their arguments, and remembers Hillel especially for his patience.

how: Jews study Hillel's answer in the Talmud, Shabbat 31a, and it is often taught to children as a first summary of Jewish ethics, always together with its last words: go and learn.

o: go, learn: Hillel's send-off after his summary

games.q: you're Hillel. a stranger asks you to teach the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. what do you do?
o: send him away, as Shammai did.
give him one line, and tell him to go and learn the rest.
tell him it can't be done.
games.why: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. that is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. now go and learn.

practice: If you can, stand on one foot; if standing isn't right for you, sit tall and lift one hand instead. Find your balance and say quietly: what is hateful to me, I won't do to my neighbor, and wobble if you wobble.
Then put your foot down, breathe, and think of one thing you'd hate someone to do to you that you might be tempted to do to someone else.

wordCard.voice: Zil g'mor, Aramaic for go, learn. Hillel's last words to the man standing on one foot, after summing up the whole Torah in a single line.

orig.note: Aramaic, zil g'mor: go, learn. Hillel's last words to the man on one foot.

carryVoice: Your line: now go and learn. The summary is short, and the learning is long. Fifty-seven days, and counting.
